title: Finding a church
hookLine: look for worship, word, welcome and love; any tradition will do the path's work
tomorrow: the home choir is splitting over a fight. does Grace stay or go?

cards: A folding table at a campus fair, a clipboard, a stranger with a friendly face: come with me Sunday. Do you go? In John's Gospel, two followers of John the Baptist start walking behind Jesus.
He turns and asks them: what seek ye? They answer with a question: where dwellest thou? He doesn't hand them a test.
He says: come and see. Christians still disagree, kindly, about what to look for once you go.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: ASK FOR THE OLD PATHS.
teach.b: Two views, both inside the church. The first says: ask for the old paths.
Jeremiah puts it this way: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls.”
Stay with the tradition that formed you, or the parish where you live, and let it shape you over years, dull Sundays included.
Its best case: a church isn't a product to shop for, and staying put lets people know you, and you them.

teach.h: VIEW TWO: LOOK FOR THE MARKS.
teach.b: The second view says: look for the marks Acts gives the first church in Jerusalem: “And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.”
Worship, word, welcome, and a love that shares with anyone in need. Find those, whatever the sign out front says.
Its best case: Christians gather in many shapes, Orthodox liturgy, a Catholic Mass, a Protestant service with hymns, a living room, and any of them can do this path's work.
Traditions answer differently what makes a church, and this path ranks none of them. Both views start in the same place.
When Nathanael scoffs, “Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?”, Philip doesn't argue.

how: Christians find a church in many ways: some visit several services, some go where family or friends worship, some join the parish or congregation nearest home; Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant churches welcome visitors to their services.

o: joining only after mastering every one of its beliefs
picking whichever one has the biggest building in town
looking for worship, word, welcome and love, then visiting

games.q: come and see — tap the pairs.
p: can any good thing come out of Nazareth?

s: Jesus answered the two followers with a list of beliefs
he asked what they sought, then said “come and see.”
Acts names doctrine, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayers
the church in Jerusalem continued steadfastly in all four.
he didn't argue; he said “come and see.”

games.q: your new roommate says, 'just go wherever the welcome feels best.' state the other view, the old paths, at its strongest.
o: staying in one tradition for years lets it form you, and lets people truly know you.
new churches are always wrong, so it's safer never to try one.
the old paths win because their buildings are the oldest.
games.why: Jeremiah: ask for the old paths, where is the good way. its best case is formation and being known. the other view looks for the marks in Acts 2:42. this path ranks neither.

practice: Stand and walk slowly to a door or a window, about a minute's worth of steps. As you go, picture a church you pass often, or one a friend belongs to, and the four things to watch for: worship, word, welcome, love.
If you pray, ask to be led to the right door.

wordCard.voice: Finding a church. Going to see for yourself, and watching for worship, word, welcome and love.

orig.note: Philip's 'come and see' to Nathanael, in the Greek of John 1:46.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: come and see, no test at the door, just a visit. That's day seventeen forty-six.
